paras: The attempted lynching of Noah Parks was the hanging of a Black preacher by a mob in Winston County, Mississippi, in the summer of 1882. Accused of stealing corn, Parks was taken from his house at night and hanged to a tree, but friends cut him down and revived him. The story ran nationally as a brief wire item, and at least one Western paper treated it as a completed lynching and endorsed it.

According to a dispatch from Jackson dated July 20, Parks, 'a colored preacher', was hanged by a mob in Winston County the night before and left for dead. A fuller version carried by weekly papers said that 'a number of men' broke into his house on July 19, dragged him out of bed, put a rope around his neck and strung him up to a tree. An Ohio summary added that he was hanged 'several times by the thumbs and finally by the neck, until he was almost dead.'

Friends cut him down 'the moment the lynchers left' and resuscitated him, while one later Virginia summary credited his wife with saving his life. The stated reason was that he was 'suspected of stealing corn'; no charge against him is reported.
No report of arrests, an inquest, or any legal action against the mob appears in the coverage, and no later news of Parks was found.

The Jackson dispatch reached daily papers from Dakota to California and Washington on July 20 and 21 under heads such as 'Lynch Law', 'Rescued in Time' and 'Preacher Hanged for Stealing Corn'. Several printings ended with the flat statement 'He stole corn', presenting the accusation as fact, and a Sacramento news summary said only that he was hanged 'for stealing earn [corn]', without the rescue. A second wire version garbled the dateline to 'Winston City' or 'Minton City', North Carolina, and a Vermont summary renamed him 'Rev. Noah Granger'.

The Salt Lake Herald wrote that a Mississippi preacher had been 'lynched by his neighbors' and that 'His offense justified the punishment', filling the paragraph with stereotypes about Black ministers and henhouses. Mississippi weeklies, including the Southern Herald of Liberty and the Brookhaven Ledger, ran the item as state news without comment in late July and early August. In September a Montana weekly reprinted it, placed in 'Winchester county', inside a column titled 'Funny Recordings'.

The date is uncertain: the Memphis Appeal of July 5 quoted the 'Winstall Signal' describing 'Noel Parks', a colored minister in Winston, hanged twice by the thumbs and once by the neck 'the other night', two weeks before the wire's July 19 date. That local item, with the same accusation that he had taken corn from 'some one else's corn-crib', suggests the attack occurred in late June or early July and was relayed late by telegraph. The victim's name also varied, appearing as 'Noah Sharks' in two Washington papers.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Noah Parks
bases: A mob took a Black preacher from his house at night and hanged him by the neck to a tree, leaving him for dead, but he was cut down and revived, making this an attempted lynching (A1, A2, A22).

Every news account says Parks was cut down and resuscitated (A1, A2, A7, A27); a 'number of men' or 'mob' hanged him without legal authority on suspicion of stealing corn (A22, A3), so this was an attempted, not a completed, lynching.
A Mississippi local paper quoted in the Memphis Appeal (A1) and the separate Jackson wire dispatches (A2, A7) agree on the victim, county, corn accusation, hanging and rescue.

framing.detail: Most dailies ran the Jackson dispatch as a short item under heads like 'Lynch Law', 'Rescued in Time' and 'Preacher Hanged for Stealing Corn', several stating the theft as fact.
The Salt Lake Herald said 'His offense justified the punishment' and filled a paragraph with stereotypes of Black preachers stealing chickens.
The Memphis Appeal's quoted local item joked that he had been 'taking up a collection out of some one else's corn-crib'.
Mississippi weeklies ran it as state news, 'suspected of stealing corn', without comment.

conflicts.note: The local item quoted on July 5 describes the same victim, county, corn accusation and hanging by thumbs and neck, so the July 20 wire's 'last night' may be a late relay of an earlier event; the local account is earlier and closer to the source.
